name: Liver Yang Rising
description: Liver Yang Rising (Gān Yáng Shàng Kàng, 肝阳上亢) is a full/empty TCM pattern affecting the Liver. Key signs: Dizziness and vertigo, Head feels heavy while feet ...
key_signs: ["Dizziness and vertigo", "Head feels heavy while feet feel light and unsteady", "Throbbing or distending headache", "Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)", "Flushed face and red eyes", "Irritability and quick temper", "Difficulty sleeping with vivid dreams", "Lower back and knee soreness and weakness", "Dry mouth and throat", "Feeling of heat rising to the face", "Heart palpitations", "Forgetfulness and poor memory", "Blurred vision or visual disturbances", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Nausea or the urge to vomit", "Hearing loss or muffled hearing", "Numbness or tingling in the hands and feet", "Stiffness in the neck and upper back", "Night sweats", "Feeling unsteady when walking, as if on a rocking boat", "Chest tightness or fullness along the ribs", "Dry eyes", "Dark or scanty urine", "Constipation or dry stools", "Hot flushes (especially in menopausal women)", "Feeling mentally restless or agitated", "Sensitivity to bright light"]
worse_with: ["Anger, frustration, or emotional stress", "Overwork or excessive mental strain", "Lack of sleep or staying up late", "Spicy, greasy, or fried foods", "Alcohol consumption", "Spring season", "Excessive sexual activity", "Loud or chaotic environments", "Bright lights", "Standing up quickly"]
better_with: ["Rest and quiet", "Lying down", "Cooling foods (celery, mung beans, chrysanthemum tea)", "Gentle, slow exercise (tai chi, walking)", "Adequate sleep and early bedtime", "Emotional calm and relaxation", "Meditation or deep breathing"]
timing_worsening_explanation: Symptoms tend to be worse in the late afternoon and evening, as Yang naturally rises during these hours. The pattern often flares in spring, when the Liver's Wood energy is naturally at its peak. Headaches and dizziness are commonly aggravated during periods of stress, after arguments, or following sleep deprivation. In the Chinese organ-clock system, the Liver is most active between 1-3 AM, and people with this pattern often find themselves waking during these hours or having restless, dream-disturbed sleep. Symptoms may worsen around menstruation in women, when Blood and Yin are further depleted. Historically, one clinical case noted that dizziness intensified at midday when Yang is at its zenith.
practitioner_notes:
Liver Yang Rising is one of the most frequently encountered patterns in clinical practice and is a textbook example of a 'mixed' or 'upper excess, lower deficiency' pattern. The diagnostic logic rests on identifying two simultaneous layers: signs of excess rising to the head and face (headache, dizziness, flushed face, irritability) combined with signs of deficiency in the lower body (weak lower back and knees, unsteady gait, deep fatigue).
The key diagnostic question is: why is the Yang rising? The root cause is almost always insufficient Yin in the Liver and Kidneys. Yin is the cooling, anchoring, nourishing aspect of the body. When it becomes depleted — through chronic stress, ageing, overwork, or long-standing emotional strain — it can no longer hold the Liver's Yang energy in check. The unmoored Yang then rises upward along the Liver channel to the head, producing the characteristic upper-body symptoms. This is why the classical texts describe it as 'Yin deficient below, Yang hyperactive above.'
Distinguishing this pattern from Liver Fire Blazing is critical. Both feature headaches, red face, and irritability, but Liver Fire is a pure excess pattern with a shorter, more acute course, prominent bitter taste, burning rib pain, constipation, and dark urine. Liver Yang Rising has a longer, more gradual course and always includes lower-body deficiency signs like weak knees and lower back soreness. The tongue and pulse also differ: Liver Fire shows a red tongue with thick yellow coating and a forceful rapid wiry pulse, while Liver Yang Rising typically shows a red tongue with thin or scanty coating and a wiry pulse that may also be fine.
pathophysiology: Depleted Liver and Kidney Yin can no longer anchor the Liver's Yang, which escapes upward to the head, causing headache, dizziness, and irritability above while the lower body remains weak and unsupported.
treatment_principle: Calm the Liver and subdue rising Yang, nourish Yin to anchor Yang
typical_timeline: 4-8 weeks for acute flare-ups to stabilize, 3-6 months to address the underlying Yin Deficiency root. Some people with deep constitutional tendencies may need periodic maintenance treatment over longer periods.
formula_modifications:
Tian Ma Gou Teng Yin Modifications- If the headache is severe and throbbing: Add Ju Hua (Chrysanthemum), Xia Ku Cao (Prunella), Zhen Zhu Mu (Pearl shell), and Ku Ding Cha (Ilex tea) to strengthen the head-clearing and Yang-subduing effect.
- If there is significant dizziness with nausea, a sense of heaviness in the head, and a thin, weak pulse: Add Gui Ban (Tortoise plastron) and consider combining with Qi Ju Di Huang Wan to nourish the deeper Yin deficiency.
- If the person is very irritable with a bitter taste in the mouth, red eyes, and constipation: Add Long Dan Cao (Gentian), Da Huang (Rhubarb), and Ze Xie (Alisma) to clear the Liver Fire that is developing alongside the rising Yang.
- If there is difficulty sleeping or very restless sleep: Add Ye Jiao Teng (Polygonum vine, already in the base formula, increase dose), Yuan Zhi (Polygala), and Suan Zao Ren (Ziziphus) to calm the Heart spirit.
- If the person also feels very tired, weak in the lower back and knees, with a thin pulse: Add Sheng Di Huang (Raw Rehmannia), Gou Qi Zi (Lycium), and He Shou Wu (Polygonum multiflorum) to more strongly nourish Liver and Kidney Yin.
- If the face feels hot and flushed: Add Di Gu Pi (Lycium bark) and Bai Wei (Cynanchum) to cool deficiency Heat from the surface.
- If there is numbness or trembling of the limbs (early internal Wind signs): Add Gui Ban (Tortoise plastron), Sheng Long Gu (raw Dragon bone), and Sheng Mu Li (raw Oyster shell) to increase the anchoring and Wind-extinguishing strength.

causes_details: [{"cause_title": "Prolonged emotional stress, frustration, and anger", "explanation": "The Liver system in TCM is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body and is deeply connected to the emotions. When a person experiences chronic stress, ongoing frustration, resentment, or frequent outbursts of anger, the Liver's smooth flow is disrupted. Qi becomes stuck (a condition called Liver Qi Stagnation), and over time this stagnation generates Heat, much like friction generates warmth. This Heat dries out and consumes the Liver's nourishing Yin fluids. As the Yin becomes depleted, it loses its ability to keep the Liver's Yang anchored, and the Yang escapes upward, causing symptoms in the head and upper body."}, {"cause_title": "Kidney Yin Deficiency from ageing or overwork", "explanation": "In TCM, the Kidney system stores the body's essential reserves and is the root source of Yin for all other organs, including the Liver. As people age, these reserves naturally decline. Similarly, chronic overwork, excessive mental strain, or a demanding lifestyle gradually drains Kidney Yin. Because the Liver and Kidney share a deep connection (often described as 'sharing the same source'), when Kidney Yin becomes depleted, it can no longer nourish and moisten the Liver. This is described as 'Water failing to nourish Wood'. Without this grounding Yin support, Liver Yang loses its anchor and rises uncontrolled to the head."}, {"cause_title": "Excessive sexual activity or chronic illness depleting Kidney essence", "explanation": "Sexual activity, from the TCM perspective, draws on Kidney essence (Jing). When this is excessive relative to a person's constitution, or when chronic illness has been slowly draining the body's reserves, Kidney essence and Yin become depleted. This weakens the Kidney's ability to produce the Yin needed to nourish the Liver, setting the stage for Liver Yang to rise unchecked. This cause is particularly relevant for people who develop this pattern at a younger age."}, {"cause_title": "Diet: spicy, greasy, or alcohol-heavy diet", "explanation": "Regularly eating hot, spicy foods, excessively oily or greasy foods, and drinking too much alcohol can generate internal Heat and Dampness. Alcohol in particular is considered warm and pungent, and tends to inflame the Liver. Greasy food can create Dampness that transforms into Heat over time. This dietary Heat directly fans Liver Yang and also damages Yin fluids, weakening the body's cooling, anchoring capacity and allowing Yang to rise."}, {"cause_title": "Liver Qi Stagnation transforming into Fire and damaging Yin", "explanation": "This is the most common internal pathway. Liver Qi Stagnation (from emotional causes) persists and gradually transforms into Liver Fire (a more intense, active Heat pattern). The Fire then burns and consumes the Liver's Yin and Blood. As these nourishing substances are depleted, they can no longer keep Yang rooted. This progression from Qi Stagnation to Fire to Yin Deficiency to Yang Rising often unfolds over months or years and explains why this pattern is typically chronic."}]

formulas.name: Tian Ma Gou Teng Yin
formulas.description: Tian Ma Gou Teng Yin (Gastrodia and Uncaria Decoction) from the Zhong Yi Nei Ke Za Bing Zheng Zhi Xin Yi is the primary formula for Liver Yang Rising with some Heat signs. It calms the Liver, extinguishes Wind, clears Heat, and nourishes the Liver and Kidneys. Composed of Tian Ma, Gou Teng, Shi Jue Ming, Zhi Zi, Huang Qin, Chuan Niu Xi, Du Zhong, Yi Mu Cao, Sang Ji Sheng, Ye Jiao Teng, and Zhu Fu Shen.

formulas.name: Zhen Gan Xi Feng Tang
formulas.description: Zhen Gan Xi Feng Tang (Settle the Liver and Extinguish Wind Decoction) from Zhang Xichun's Yi Xue Zhong Zhong Can Xi Lu is used when Liver Yang Rising is more severe, with pronounced upward surging of Qi and Blood and early signs of internal Wind such as limb numbness, unsteady gait, or a flushed face 'as if intoxicated'. It uses heavy substances like Niu Xi, Dai Zhe Shi, Long Gu, and Mu Li to strongly anchor rising Yang.

formulas.name: Qi Ju Di Huang Wan
formulas.description: Qi Ju Di Huang Wan (Lycium Berry, Chrysanthemum, and Rehmannia Pill) is used when the underlying Liver and Kidney Yin Deficiency is the dominant feature, with milder Yang Rising symptoms. It nourishes Liver and Kidney Yin as the root treatment, with Gou Qi Zi and Ju Hua specifically clearing the head and eyes.

formulas.name: Huang Long Tang
formulas.description: Jian Ling Tang (Construct Pitcher Decoction) from the Yi Xue Zhong Zhong Can Xi Lu is suited for Liver Yang Rising with prominent insomnia and restlessness but without severe Qi-Blood rebellion. It combines heavy subduing substances with heart-calming herbs like Bai Zi Ren.

herbs.name: Tian Ma
herbs.description: Tian Ma (Gastrodia) enters the Liver channel and is one of the premier herbs for calming Liver Yang and extinguishing internal Wind. It directly addresses the headache and dizziness that define this pattern.

herbs.name: Gou Teng
herbs.description: Gou Teng (Uncaria) clears Heat from the Liver channel and calms Liver Yang. Paired with Tian Ma, it is one of the most commonly used herb combinations for this pattern.

herbs.name: Shi Jue Ming
herbs.description: Shi Jue Ming (Abalone shell) is a heavy mineral-shell substance that weighs down and anchors rising Liver Yang. Its salty, cold nature is ideal for subduing Yang and clearing Liver Heat.

herbs.name: Bai Shao
herbs.description: Bai Shao (White Peony root) nourishes Liver Blood and Yin, softening the Liver's rigid nature. By replenishing the Yin substance, it helps anchor Yang so it does not flare upward.

herbs.name: Long Gu
herbs.description: Long Gu (Dragon bone) is a heavy, settling substance that calms the spirit and anchors floating Yang. It is commonly used alongside Mu Li (Oyster shell) for this purpose.

herbs.name: Mu Li Ke
herbs.description: Mu Li (Oyster shell) subdues Yang, calms the spirit, and softens hardness. Its heavy, salty nature helps drag rising Yang back down and settle restless Heart spirit disturbed by the ascending Yang.

herbs.name: Ju Hua
herbs.description: Ju Hua (Chrysanthemum flower) clears the Liver and brightens the eyes. It is gentle enough for long-term use and specifically addresses eye symptoms and headache from Liver Yang Rising.

herbs.name: Gou Qi Zi
herbs.description: Gou Qi Zi (Goji berry) nourishes Liver and Kidney Yin, addressing the root deficiency that allows Yang to rise unchecked. Gentle and tonifying, it is suitable for sustained use.

herbs.name: Dai Zhe Shi
herbs.description: Dai Zhe Shi (Hematite) is a heavy mineral that strongly subdues rebellious Qi and redirects it downward. It is used when Yang rising is more severe, especially with marked head distension and flushing.

acupoints.name: Taichong LR-3
acupoints.description: Taichong LIV-3, the source point of the Liver channel, is the single most important point for this pattern. It calms the Liver, subdues rising Yang, regulates Qi flow, and brings hyperactive Liver energy back down. Needled with reducing method.

acupoints.name: Taixi KI-3
acupoints.description: Taixi KID-3, the source point of the Kidney channel, nourishes Kidney Yin to address the root deficiency. By strengthening the Water element, it helps anchor and control the rising Wood (Liver) Yang. Needled with reinforcing method.

acupoints.name: Fengchi GB-20
acupoints.description: Fengchi GB-20, at the base of the skull where the Gallbladder channel ascends, directly addresses headache, dizziness, eye problems, and neck stiffness caused by Liver Yang surging upward to the head. Needled with reducing method.

acupoints.name: Baihui DU-20
acupoints.description: Baihui DU-20, at the crown of the head where all Yang channels converge, subdues rising Yang and clears the head. It is especially useful for dizziness and a heavy, distended feeling in the head.

acupoints.name: Xingjian LR-2
acupoints.description: Xingjian LIV-2, the Ying-Spring (Fire) point of the Liver channel, clears Liver Fire and drains excess Heat from the channel. It is selected when the Yang Rising is accompanied by more obvious Heat signs like red eyes, irritability, and a bitter taste.

acupoints.name: Xiaxi GB-43
acupoints.description: Xiaxi GB-43, the Ying-Spring point of the Gallbladder channel, clears Heat from the Gallbladder and Liver, addresses tinnitus and temporal headache. It helps drain excess from the Shao Yang level.

acupoints.name: Neiguan PC-6
acupoints.description: Neiguan P-6 calms the Heart spirit, eases irritability and insomnia, and helps subdue Liver Yang. As a Luo-connecting point linked to the Yin Wei Mai, it has a broad settling and calming effect.

faqs.question: What is Liver Yang Rising in TCM?
faqs.answer: Depleted Liver and Kidney Yin can no longer anchor the Liver's Yang, which escapes upward to the head, causing headache, dizziness, and irritability above while the lower body remains weak and unsupported.

faqs.question: What are the key signs of Liver Yang Rising?
faqs.answer: Key signs include: Dizziness and vertigo, Head feels heavy while feet feel light and unsteady, Throbbing or distending headache, Ringing in the ears (tinnitus), Flushed face and red eyes, Irritability and quick temper, Difficulty sleeping with vivid dreams, Lower back and knee soreness and weakness, Dry mouth and throat, Feeling of heat rising to the face, Heart palpitations, Forgetfulness and poor memory.

faqs.question: What formulas treat Liver Yang Rising?
faqs.answer: Common formulas for Liver Yang Rising include: Tian Ma Gou Teng Yin, Zhen Gan Xi Feng Tang, Qi Ju Di Huang Wan, Huang Long Tang.

faqs.question: What Western conditions relate to Liver Yang Rising?
faqs.answer: This pattern is associated with: Essential hypertension, Migraine, Tension headache, Meniere's disease, Tinnitus, Insomnia, Perimenopause / Menopausal syndrome, Transient ischemic attack, Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.

faqs.question: What is the treatment principle for Liver Yang Rising?
faqs.answer: Calm the Liver and subdue rising Yang, nourish Yin to anchor Yang
